palmitoyl-tripeptide-8.text: Skincare users with sensitive or reddish skin look to this peptide (sold as Neutrazen) to calm irritation and reduce visible redness for a more even-looking face. It is promoted for this in cosmetics; standalone human data for that use are essentially absent.

palmitoyl-hexapeptide-12.text: Anti-aging cream users choose this elastin-derived peptide (Biopeptide EL) hoping for firmer, more elastic skin and a smoother look. The evidence for that use sits at lab level, and no clinical trials were found.

palmitoyl-oligopeptide.text: Palmitoyl oligopeptide is a generic label on anti-aging creams, where it is described as a collagen-promoting signal ingredient meant to give firmer, smoother-looking skin. The collagen claim appears in patent literature; no clinical trial of the ingredient itself was found.

manganese-tripeptide-1.text: Users of facial serums reach for this manganese analogue of GHK to address sun damage and dark spots and even out skin tone. One small study sits behind the use, so the evidence for the brightening effect is limited.

tripeptide-3.text: Oily-skin users see tripeptide-3 in products marketed for oil control, aiming for a less shiny, more matte face. Published evidence under this name is thin, limited to one small 2024 delivery study.

tripeptide-10-citrulline.text: Anti-aging skincare users seek this peptide (Decorinyl) for tidier collagen fibres and firmer, smoother skin. Support comes from in vitro data and one 24-person study.

acetyl-hexapeptide-3.text: Known as Argireline, this peptide is promoted as a topical alternative to Botox for softening expression lines around the eyes and forehead. It has been studied in humans for wrinkle depth, with modest and inconsistent results.

acetyl-tetrapeptide-15.text: Used in products for sensitive or reactive skin (sold as Skinasensyl), it is promoted as reducing nerve-driven irritation so skin looks calmer. Evidence is supplier data only; no independent studies were found.

acetyl-tetrapeptide-2.text: Marketed in skin-firming and anti-aging products (such as Thymulen 4), it is claimed to support epidermal regeneration for firmer skin. Evidence consists of cell-culture data and one combination-lotion hair study, not a skin-firmness trial.

acetyl-dipeptide-1-cetyl-ester.text: Sensitive-skin users choose this soothing peptide (Calmosensine) to reduce stinging and redness for a calmer complexion. Supplier data support it, while one head-to-head trial found no significant stinging benefit.

pentapeptide-18.text: Sold as Leuphasyl, this enkephalin-mimic is promoted as a 'Botox-like' ingredient to soften expression lines. Human evidence comes from a retinol combination cream, so its separate contribution is untested.

pentapeptide-3.text: The name is ambiguous: formerly the KTTKS collagen peptide (Matrixyl), and linked to Vialox, a 'Botox-like' ingredient. Users take it for smoother, less lined skin; verified evidence for either use is scarce.

oligopeptide-68.text: Skin-brightening serum users take this peptide to fade dark spots and melasma and even out tone. Human data are small melasma studies of multi-ingredient products.

tetrapeptide-21.text: This GEKG peptide appears in anti-aging skincare for collagen support and firmer-looking skin. Research so far covers skin delivery and cell-culture effects rather than human trials.

acetyl-tetrapeptide-3.text: Used in topical products for thinning hair, usually within the Capixyl blend with biochanin A and ginseng, to look for thicker, fuller hair. It was tested only inside a multi-herbal combination against 3% minoxidil in one small trial.

palmitoyl-tetrapeptide-3.text: Appears in serum ingredient lists as a signal peptide, where users expect smoother, firmer-looking skin. It is found in patent compositions with plant extracts; no published human trials exist for it.

deoxyarbutin.text: Used as a topical lightener to fade age spots, melasma and other dark patches for a more even tone. Evidence comes mostly from lab and animal work, with thin human trial data.

aloesin.text: This Aloe-derived compound is studied as a topical lightener for dark spots and uneven tone. Evidence for that use is lab-level, and no published trials were found.

ellagic-acid.text: This fruit and nut polyphenol appears in some skin-care products as a brightener, and users take it as an antioxidant. No skin trials were found for the brightening use.

4-n-butylresorcinol.text: Used in serums and creams for melasma and age spots to even out tone. Several small randomized trials have reported improvement for this use.

rhododendrol.text: Developed as a skin-lightening cosmetic ingredient to brighten tone, it was used until July 2013, when it was withdrawn after reports of patchy depigmentation. It is documented here as a historical product.

monobenzone.text: A prescription depigmenting cream used for extensive vitiligo so remaining skin matches the pale patches. Forums discuss it as a permanent route to lighter skin, though that use outside vitiligo is off-label and the effect is described as irreversible.

oxyresveratrol.text: This mulberry-derived stilbene is discussed as a skin-lightening ingredient for dark spots and uneven tone. Its tyrosinase inhibition is shown in the lab; no human skin trials back the brightening claims.

resveratrol-topical.text: Used in anti-aging and brightening serums as an antioxidant for a fresher, more even look. Evidence includes one small recent trial, with most research focused on delivery formulations.

licochalcone-a.text: This licorice-root compound appears in products for sensitive, red or acne-prone skin and is also discussed for possible brightening via pigment reduction. Lab work hints at tyrosinase inhibition, and human trials are combination-product acne studies.

chitosan.text: Sold as a fat-binding supplement for weight loss, and used as a carrier in cosmetics. No trial shows a skin-pigment or appearance effect from it.

diacetyl-boldine.text: Found in serums for hyperpigmentation, dark spots and melasma, usually as one part of a multi-ingredient formula. Evidence is small combination-formula studies, with no stand-alone trials.

mulberry-extract.text: Marketed in skincare as a botanical brightener for a more even tone. Published research concerns blood sugar and antioxidants, not skin tone.

rice-bran-extract.text: Popular in K-beauty and J-beauty products for brightening, moisturizing and antioxidant effects. Evidence includes antioxidant and cell-culture data, with no controlled human skin-tone trial found.

flutamide-topical-melasma.text: An oral prostate-cancer antiandrogen, studied off-label as a 1% topical for melasma to even out facial pigmentation. The evidence base for that use is thin.
